Prior authorization checks that applicable Medicare coverage, payment and coding requirements are met before the item is delivered. ## How items are selected CMS keeps a Master List of DMEPOS items that may require prior authorization or a face-to-face encounter with a written order before delivery. The list is updated at least once a year based on items with patterns of unnecessary utilization. Items on the Required Prior Authorization List are chosen by evaluating DMEPOS categories for problematic billing trends. Recent additions include orthoses, power mobility devices, pressure reducing support surfaces, lower limb prosthetics and pneumatic compression devices. Selected items usually start in some geographic regions and then expand nationwide.

results.text:
AI. Follow-up visits use codes 99307-99310. Nurse practitioners, clinical nurse specialists and certified nurse midwives may perform initial visits where state law permits and collaboration and supervision requirements are met. Office and outpatient: physicians and qualified nonphysician practitioners choose a new or established patient visit code (99201-99215) based on visit complexity and the patient relationship. A new patient is one who has not received professional services from the physician or physician group practice within the previous 3 years.

Critical Access Hospital Method II: appropriate new or established visit codes (99201-99215) are reported on type of bill 85X with revenue codes 96X, 97X or 98X for physicians and nonphysician practitioners with reassigned billing rights.

Rural Health Clinics and Federally Qualified Health Centers: consultation codes were discontinued in favor of office visit codes (99201-99215) and nursing facility codes (99304-99306) as appropriate.

final_text:
**Claim 637252 has a low denial risk in this model.** The model gives it a probability of denial of 0.055. The validation-set average is 0.1805, so the claim scores 0.3 times that average, or -12.6 percentage points. The denial label in this project is synthetic. The score is for a constructed label, not for a real payer decision.

**What the model weighs.** This is a carrier claim. Every feature the model weighs most heavily lowers the risk:
- **Principal diagnosis Z733** (Z73.3, Stress, not elsewhere classified) has the largest effect. It lowers the odds of denial by 33%.
- **HCPCS code 96127** lowers the odds by 22%. It is a CPT code, and this project doesn't carry CPT descriptions, so I can't say what the service is.
- **Place of service 11** (Office) lowers the odds by 16%.
- **Billing provider NPI, referring PIN and TAX_NUM** each lower the odds by 5–7%. The referring PIN field is undocumented in the project dictionary, so I can't say what it means. The NPI and TIN values are synthetic.

The other 153 features together add a small further reduction.

The model also reported one unseen category value on this claim. That makes the score somewhat less certain.

**What to check before submitting.** The policy documents I searched don't cover CPT 96127 or this diagnosis. They cover only the consultation-code rule (CMS Transmittal 1875), CPAP, and DMEPOS prior authorization. Nothing in them applies to this claim, so I can't give a policy-based checklist. A general review is still reasonable. Confirm that the codes and the place of service match the documentation, and check the payer's own rules for 96127. Also find out which field was the unseen category value.
